target_customer: Home fitness consumers who want boxing and kickboxing workouts with punch tracking, paying for hardware and a subscription
problem: People who box for fitness could not measure punches or progress at home, and gym boxing classes are costly and fixed in time and place.
business_model: Connected fitness: hardware kits (punch trackers, bag, gloves) plus a monthly content subscription

founders.name: Khalil Zahar
education: Graduate student studying microelectromechanical systems (per company about page; school not stated)
founders.background_notes: Began boxing in 2010 and built a tracker after his progress plateaued, per the company about page.

founders.name: Alexandre Marcotte
founders.background_notes: Company blog says he and Zahar began the first prototype in 2014.

founders.name: Patrick Chandler
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him as Founder/CMO with paid social and content marketing experience.

founders.name: Jerome Soucy Rousseau
founders.background_notes: Named co-founder on the company about page.

founders.name: Tommy Duquette
founders.background_notes: Joined in late 2015 per the October 2019 company blog; named co-founder there and on the about page.

founders.name: Alexandre Lapointe
founders.background_notes: Named co-founder on the company about page.

technical_complexity.rationale: Small wearable motion sensors with punch recognition needed embedded hardware, signal processing and app work, which is standard but nontrivial for a small team; a connected content platform came later.

defensibility.rationale: Proprietary sensors, tracking algorithms and trainer content were moderately hard to copy, though comparable punch tracking and virtual boxing classes could be built by others.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Press compared it to Peloton for punching (CNBC 2018, TechCrunch 2021) but no incumbent bought or copied it in sources found.

market_need_then: No dated 2016 source on demand was found; the company says boxers had no way to measure improvement and that sensors had become small enough to wear. Later press (2021) frames a boxing and connected fitness boom.

branding.domain_note: Used joinfightcamp.com as the main domain (also fightcamp.com appears in search results).

identity.logo: Custom lettering wordmark (per a low authority font blog)
identity.visual_style: October 2019 refresh keeps a clean approachable look and adds the bold style of vintage boxing posters
identity.voice_and_tone: Authentic, fighter focused: Train like a Fighter

branding.brand_signature: Train like a Fighter, with real coaches and punch tracking leaderboards

rebrands.why: Company says it wanted authenticity in boxing and to reach a wider audience.

branding.community_and_virality: Celebrity investors (Mike Tyson, Floyd Mayweather and others) generated press in 2021 and reviews call it the Peloton of punching bags; leaderboards are a core feature.

brand_strength.rationale: Strong category association and celebrity backing reported in 2021, but the company legal name stayed Hykso and no source shows brand driven growth.

pivots.why: CNBC (January 25 2018) says Hykso was moving beyond punch tracking hardware to on-demand training videos at home.

outcome_analysis: FightCamp began as a punch tracking sensor made by Hykso, added a coached subscription library in 2018 and benefited from the 2020 and 2021 home fitness boom, raising a 90 million dollar round in June 2021 led by NEA and Connect Ventures with about 98 million raised in total per TechCrunch. No acquisition or shutdown appears in sources found, though connected fitness demand cooled after 2021.
notes: TechCrunch says about 8M was raised before the 90M round (total 98M), but those earlier rounds were not found, so they are not recorded; CB Insights (aggregator) says 94.7M over 8 rounds and calls the 90M round a Series B while a Crowell and Moring deal note mentions a 50M Series B dated July 2021, a conflict left unresolved. TechCrunch does not label the 90M stage so it is stored as other. Founder lists differ between the YC page (three) and the company about page (six); the company page was used. Education details come only from the about page. No dated competitor source near the 2016 batch was found, so the list is empty; Peloton is mentioned as a comparison in 2018 and 2021 press only. A search summary says the company launched as Hykso and later became FightCamp; I could not verify this in a page I opened (the footer lists Hykso, Inc.), so no name rebrand is recorded. Earlier 8M round added with null date and no investors: it rests on one outlet, TechCrunch, where the company says it had raised 8M before the 90M round (total 98M). IVP and Left Lane Capital were kept because sources confirm them: Foley lists IVP among additional investors in the round, and Athletech News names Left Lane (quoting Left Lane's founder), though TechCrunch itself lists neither.
